title: Environmental Sensors, Placement, Calibration and Data Quality

content.overview: Environmental numbers are only useful when the measurement represents the crop. Sensor location, shielding, calibration, airflow exposure, and logging interval can all change what a temperature or humidity reading means.

vocabulary.definition: Comparison and adjustment of a measuring instrument against a known reference or standard.
A systematic measurement error that consistently shifts readings away from the true condition.
A measurement position chosen to reflect the environment actually experienced by the crop rather than an atypical hot, cold, wet, or dry zone.

sections.title: Placement determines relevance
sections.body: A sensor near a dehumidifier outlet, wall, lamp, intake, or wet surface may report a local microclimate rather than the average crop environment. Placement should be selected to answer a defined question about the canopy.

sections.title: Calibration protects trend quality
sections.body: Two sensors can drift apart over time. Periodic comparison with a reliable reference helps distinguish real environmental change from instrument error.

sections.title: Logging reveals dynamics
sections.body: Short-term peaks, nighttime transitions, irrigation events, and equipment cycling can disappear inside a daily average. Logged data should preserve enough time resolution to reveal biologically meaningful patterns.

workedExamples: If one humidity sensor reads much drier than the others, compare its location and calibration before changing the room set point.
A room average can look acceptable while a sensor inside a dense canopy shows prolonged high humidity; investigate the local microclimate rather than relying only on the wall controller.

Two canopy sensors differ by 7% RH. Instead of averaging them immediately, compare their height, shielding, nearby airflow, calibration history and logging interval to decide whether the difference is real or measurement bias.
A daily average looks normal, but 10-minute data show repeated humidity spikes after irrigation. The higher-resolution record explains a risk pattern that the daily mean hides.
commonMistakes: Placing sensors where equipment exhaust directly affects them.
Assuming a new sensor cannot be biased.
Using a single daily average to evaluate short-term environmental stress.
Using an unshielded sensor in direct radiant load as if it represented canopy air temperature.
Comparing data from different logging intervals without noting the resolution change.
content.practicalApplication: Map sensor locations, compare readings under the same conditions, document calibration checks, and review logged temperature and humidity around important transitions such as lights-on, lights-off, irrigation, and equipment cycling.
content.summary: Good environmental control starts with trustworthy measurements. Sensor placement, calibration, and logging context determine whether temperature, humidity, and VPD data actually describe the crop.

blocks.title: A number is only useful if it represents the crop
blocks.body: Environmental control depends on measurement validity. Sensor bias, poor placement, direct radiant heating, equipment exhaust and logging choices can create values that are numerically precise but biologically misleading.

blocks.title: Common sensor errors
rows: Local microclimate mistaken for crop average

items.title: Define the question
items.body: Decide whether the sensor should represent room air, canopy air, intake air or another zone.

items.title: Inspect placement
items.body: Check height, shielding, nearby surfaces and equipment influence.

items.title: Compare sensors
items.body: Co-locate devices temporarily when drift is suspected.

items.title: Review time resolution
items.body: Make sure the logging interval can capture the events you care about.

items.title: Document changes
items.body: Record relocation, replacement or calibration so trends remain interpretable.

blocks.title: One sensor disagrees
blocks.setting: Three canopy sensors read 25.1 °C / 62% RH, 25.4 °C / 61% RH and 27.8 °C / 54% RH. The outlier is mounted near a supply-air outlet.
blocks.prompt: What is the best first action?
options: Validate the outlier's placement and calibration
Average all three and ignore the difference
blocks.answer: Validate the outlier's placement and calibration.
blocks.feedback: A local airflow effect or sensor issue should be ruled out before a room-wide correction.

blocks.title: Sensor-placement audit
blocks.instructions: Review a room diagram with sensor locations and identify which readings are likely representative.
prompts: Recommend a better location for any weak sensor.
State what logging interval would capture lights-on/off and irrigation transitions.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Trustworthy environmental control starts with representative, calibrated measurements and enough time resolution to reveal meaningful changes.

academyEnrichment.whyItMatters: Bad sensor data can make a good control strategy behave badly. Learners need to distinguish real crop-environment change from measurement error before acting.

primaryVisuals.alt: Educational sensor placement diagram comparing representative canopy sensor positions with readings biased by walls, equipment airflow and atypical microclimates, followed by a verification sequence.
primaryVisuals.caption: A valid sensor can still answer the wrong question when it is placed in an unrepresentative microclimate. Verify location and calibration before changing room controls.
